section_summary: This section documents diplomatic friction and internal political tensions arising from public depictions and constitutional interpretations of Emperor Hirohito during August through October 1935. Following the publication of a satirical cartoon in the August issue of Vanity Fair and a subsequent street burlesque in Seattle, Japanese diplomats lodged protests and sought the suppression of the magazine across the United States and China, while U.S. officials defended constitutional protections of free speech. In China, Japanese consular officials actively pressured local municipal authorities and foreign police to confiscate the magazine and prevent news coverage of the incidents. Concurrently, despatches from Tokyo analyze the domestic political crisis surrounding Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's 'organ theory' of the monarchy, which culminated in Minobe's resignation from the House of Peers and an emphatic victory for the military and imperial fundamentalists.

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull explains to the Japanese Ambassador that the U.S. government cannot curb free speech or utterances of individual citizens regarding publications deemed offensive.
subfiles.summary: In this concluding page of a memorandum of conversation, Secretary of State Cordell Hull records his discussion with the Japanese Ambassador regarding an offensive publication. Hull explained that while he regretted incidents causing displeasure to foreign governments, the United States is a country of free speech where the government cannot improperly curb individual citizens' utterances over which it lacks control. He noted that attempting to do so would cause more harm than good through resentment and bitterness, and he made no commitment regarding what he would say publicly.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Secretary of State on Conference with the Japanese Ambassador (Concluding Page)

subfiles.about: Minister Nelson T. Johnson transmits a report from the Consul General at Shanghai regarding Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki's request to suppress the August Vanity Fair in China.
subfiles.summary: Minister Nelson T. Johnson transmits a message from American Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham in Shanghai reporting an interview with Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki. Terasaki personally and informally asked for suggestions on how to prevent the August issue of Vanity Fair from circulating in China. Cunningham replied that while he disliked offending Japanese susceptibilities, he had no suggestions and was obligated to protect American commercial interests.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 406 from Peiping Transmitting Shanghai Message on Vanity Fair

subfiles.about: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs recommends taking no action regarding telegrams from Peiping and letting the Shanghai Vanity Fair issue be resolved locally.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum discusses Peiping telegrams Nos. 406 and 408 regarding Japanese requests to prevent the circulation of the August Vanity Fair in Shanghai. It notes that the American Consul General will take no affirmative action without Department authorization and that the Japanese Foreign Office appears inclined to drop the matter vis-à-vis the U.S. Government. It recommends that the Department take no action and allow the Shanghai situation to be handled and adjusted locally, a view concurred in by Mr. Ward of the Legal Adviser's Office.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Efforts to Prevent Circulation of Vanity Fair in Shanghai

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson transmits a Shanghai report that Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki requested the American Consul General to ask the Shanghai Municipal Council police to suppress Vanity Fair.
subfiles.summary: Minister Nelson T. Johnson forwards a telegram from Consul General Cunningham in Shanghai detailing a follow-up visit by Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki. Terasaki suggested that Cunningham write to the Chairman of the Shanghai Municipal Council requesting the police to suppress delivered copies of Vanity Fair and prevent further sales. Cunningham informed Terasaki that he could not take such action while fulfilling his duty to protect American interests.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 408 from Peiping Relaying Shanghai Report on Municipal Council Police

subfiles.about: A newspaper clipping reproducing the Associated Press wirephoto of the Vanity Fair cartoon of Emperor Hirohito by William Gropper.
subfiles.summary: This clipping from a Washington newspaper reproduces the Vanity Fair cartoon by artist William Gropper depicting Emperor Hirohito. The caption notes that the cartoon depicting the Emperor in an unlikely historical situation has angered Japan and prompted official protests. It also mentions other cartoons in Gropper's satirical series.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping: 'Cartoon Protested by Japan'

subfiles.about: Chargé d'Affaires Neville reports that Japanese newspaper coverage of an alleged incident of disrespect toward the Emperor in Seattle ceased following reports of Hornbeck's desire for a local settlement.
subfiles.summary: Edwin L. Neville reports from Tokyo that Japanese newspapers featured the recent alleged disrespect of the Japanese Emperor in Seattle on August 10 and 12. He observes that the press has ceased mentioning the affair following the publication of a statement that Stanley K. Hornbeck expressed to the Japanese Counselor a desire for a local settlement.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 167 from Tokyo on Seattle Disrespect Incident

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson transmits a report on Chinese bookstore bans and Japanese purchases of Vanity Fair copies in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Nelson T. Johnson relays a report from Shanghai regarding an article in the North China Daily News stating that Chinese authorities would ban bookstores from selling the August Vanity Fair at the request of Japanese consular officials. The Consul General notes that no confirmation was attempted, but ascertained that Kelly and Walsh are attempting to purchase news agency copies on behalf of the Japanese Consulate General, with total copies reaching Shanghai news agencies not exceeding twenty-five.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 416 from Peiping Concerning Sale of Vanity Fair in Shanghai

subfiles.about: Eugene H. Dooman records a conversation with Japanese Counselor Seijiro Yoshizawa regarding the official protest against the Vanity Fair caricature and the advisability of public statements.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Counselor Seijiro Yoshizawa informed Eugene H. Dooman that the Japanese Embassy had been instructed to protest officially against the caricature of Emperor Hirohito in Vanity Fair and that Ambassador Saito had met with Secretary Hull. Yoshizawa conveyed appreciation for Hull's private remarks and suggested the Secretary make a similar statement at a press conference. Dooman argued against a public statement, stating it would revive public curiosity and create a false impression of abnormal U.S.-Japan relations. Yoshizawa also noted that Vanity Fair's editor planned to send an explanatory letter to Ambassador Saito, and Dooman observed that diplomatic protests had predictably provoked sensational press coverage.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Seijiro Yoshizawa and Eugene H. Dooman

subfiles.about: A newspaper article containing interviews with cartoonist William Gropper, editor Frank Crowninshield, and reporting Ambassador Saito's return to Washington.
subfiles.summary: Cartoonist William Gropper denounces Japanese censorship demands as divine stupidity and comparable to Nazi Germany, announcing plans to publish further caricatures of Emperor Hirohito in The New Masses and other publications. Frank Crowninshield, editor of Vanity Fair, explains that the magazine is a humorous and satirical periodical that regularly lampoons leaders including President Roosevelt without malice. The article also describes Ambassador Hirosi Saito interrupting his vacation in New Canaan, Connecticut, to return to Washington to address the controversy.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping: 'Divine Stupidity... Can't Apologize' (New York Herald Tribune)

subfiles.about: An Associated Press article reporting Tokyo press outrage over the Vanity Fair cartoon and Ambassador Saito's return to Washington.
subfiles.summary: The article reports from Tokyo that the Japanese Foreign Office and press reacted with outrage to the Vanity Fair caricature of Emperor Hirohito, comparing it to the recent New Life incident in Shanghai. Japanese newspapers criticized the Washington Embassy and Yokohama customs officials for failing to prevent the cartoon's publication and entry into Japan. It also reports from Washington that Ambassador Saito cut short his Connecticut vacation to confer with officials, while U.S. State Department spokesmen noted that the American government has no legal control over the press.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping: 'Caricature Might Disturb Public Peace, Tokyo Press Angered' (Baltimore Sun)

subfiles.about: A newspaper clipping reproducing the Vanity Fair cartoon depicting Emperor Hirohito pulling a cart with the Nobel Peace Prize.
subfiles.summary: This clipping from the Washington Post reproduces the Vanity Fair caricature showing Emperor Hirohito pulling a cart carrying a scroll inscribed 'Japan's Emperor Gets the Nobel Peace Prize.' The caption notes that the cartoon depicting an unlikely historical situation has aroused official protests from the Japanese government in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping: 'Protested by Japanese' (Washington Post)

subfiles.about: An editorial cartoon by Gene Elderman in the Washington Post satirizing the U.S. balanced budget as an unlikely historical situation with apologies to Vanity Fair.
subfiles.summary: This clipping features an editorial cartoon by Gene Elderman published in the Washington Post on August 6, 1935. The cartoon depicts Uncle Sam looking through binoculars at a distant flying bird labeled 'Budget Balanced,' with the caption 'Apologies to Vanity Fair' and 'Another Unlikely Historical Situation.' The cartoon plays on the phrase and concept used in the controversial Vanity Fair feature to satirize American fiscal policy.
subfiles.title: Political Cartoon Clipping: 'Another Unlikely Historical Situation' by Elderman (Washington Post)

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits confidential memoranda of conversations concerning the Vanity Fair caricature to Consul General Peck in Nanking.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sends confidential instructions to Consul General Willys R. Peck at Nanking referring to telegram No. 234 to Peiping regarding the Vanity Fair caricature of the Japanese Emperor. Enclosed for Peck's confidential staff information is a copy of Hull's memorandum of conversation of August 5 with Ambassador Saito, along with memoranda of conversations held on August 3 and August 5 between Japanese Embassy Counselor Yoshizawa and a Department officer.
subfiles.title: Instruction to Willys R. Peck, American Consul General at Nanking

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits confidential memoranda of conversations regarding the Vanity Fair caricature to Minister Johnson in Peiping.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sends confidential instructions to American Minister Nelson T. Johnson at Peiping concerning the caricature of the Japanese Emperor in the August Vanity Fair. The despatch encloses copies of Hull's August 5 memorandum of conversation with the Japanese Ambassador and the August 3 and 5 memoranda of conversations between the Counselor of the Japanese Embassy and a Department officer.
subfiles.title: Instruction to Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Peiping

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits confidential memoranda of conversations regarding the Vanity Fair caricature to Chargé Neville in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull addresses an instruction to Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo referencing telegram No. 123 of August 5 concerning the Vanity Fair caricature. For confidential staff information, Hull encloses copies of his August 5 conversation with Ambassador Saito and Eugene H. Dooman's conversations with Counselor Yoshizawa of August 3 and August 5.
subfiles.title: Instruction to Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim at Tokyo

subfiles.about: A draft statement for the Secretary of State to deliver to the press regarding international courtesy and the Vanity Fair incident under the Good Neighbor policy.
subfiles.summary: Prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, this draft suggests a statement for Secretary Hull to give to the press concerning the Japanese caricature incident. It invokes the Good Neighbor principle, emphasizing that friendly international relations require citizens and media in every country to respect the ideas and susceptibilities of other peoples. It notes that foreign affairs would be less difficult if agencies of public expression avoided gratuitously wounding or offending other nations.
subfiles.title: Draft Press Statement on the Good Neighbor Principle and Foreign Sensitivities

subfiles.about: Consul Samuel Sokobin reports that Chinese newspapers in Tsingtao published an apology for reprinting an account of the Seattle burlesque of the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Consul Samuel Sokobin reports that leading Chinese newspaper correspondents in Tsingtao prominently published a notice apologizing for reprinting an account of the Seattle street incident involving representations of the Emperor of Japan pulling a rickshaw with the King of Ethiopia. The apology noted that the local municipal government had already prohibited reprinting the item pursuant to Japanese instructions. Sokobin adds that the same story had appeared in local English and Japanese language newspapers several days prior to its publication in the Chinese press.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 42 from Tsingtao on Chinese Newspaper Apology for Seattle Burlesque Report

subfiles.about: Eugene H. Dooman details an informal meeting with Japanese Counselor Yoshizawa concerning the Vanity Fair caricature and photograph of the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Seijiro Yoshizawa informed Eugene H. Dooman that the New York correspondent of the Osaka Asahi had alerted the Embassy to the August Vanity Fair caricature and photograph of the Japanese Emperor and Empress. Yoshizawa lodged an unofficial protest, emphasizing the sacred reverence the Japanese people hold for their Emperor and predicting public outrage in Japan. Dooman recalled a similar complaint the previous year, explaining that the U.S. government had no legal authority to suppress publications and that official intervention would only generate sensational publicity. Dooman maintained that Americans view such cartoons as harmless satire, while promising to report the matter to Hornbeck and the Under Secretary.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Seijiro Yoshizawa and Eugene H. Dooman on Vanity Fair Caricature

subfiles.about: Stanley K. Hornbeck provides recommendations and talking points for Secretary Hull's upcoming meeting with Ambassador Saito regarding the Vanity Fair caricature.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck advises Secretary Hull on handling Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito's scheduled visit to protest the Vanity Fair caricature. He recommends listening patiently and giving a noncommittal oral reply that leaves the matter open to fade away without offering an apology, while showing sympathetic understanding of Saito's difficult position amid domestic military pressure. Hornbeck provides detailed talking points emphasizing American constitutional principles of free speech, the good-natured and non-derogatory intent of the cartoon, the lack of legal power to penalize the publisher, and the risk that official action would only magnify the controversy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Anticipated Call of the Japanese Ambassador Regarding Vanity Fair Caricature

subfiles.about: Eugene H. Dooman records Japanese Counselor Yoshizawa's account of a street stunt in Seattle burlesquing the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Yoshizawa reported that an individual dressed as 'the Mikado' had pulled a cart carrying a person dressed as the Emperor of Ethiopia through the streets of Seattle during an early morning stunt. Yoshizawa recounted that the Japanese Consul in Seattle had tried to prevent the performance through the Japan Society and Chamber of Commerce, and later sought an interview with the Mayor of Seattle. Yoshizawa stated that while he was not lodging a formal protest, the Embassy was concerned about Japanese public reaction and west coast tensions, hoping for a local resolution. Dooman replied that the stunt was likely childish mischief provoked by the Vanity Fair publicity rather than malice, and urged the Embassy to avoid telling the press that representations had been made to the State Department.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Seijiro Yoshizawa and Eugene H. Dooman on the Seattle 'Mikado' Incident

subfiles.about: Under Secretary William Phillips describes a meeting with Ambassador Saito concerning the Seattle street burlesque of the Japanese Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Hirosi Saito called upon Under Secretary William Phillips under instructions from the Japanese Foreign Office regarding the Seattle burlesque incident, having previously advised Tokyo that the Mayor of Seattle's apology was sufficient. Phillips commended Saito's advice to his government and noted with satisfaction that Saito refrained from using the word 'protest.' Phillips reaffirmed Secretary Hull's previous public statement on the Vanity Fair case as adequately covering both matters, and Saito expressed satisfaction with this response.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between William Phillips and Ambassador Hirosi Saito on the Seattle Incident

subfiles.about: The Department of State informs Chargé Neville in Tokyo of conversations with the Japanese Counselor and Ambassador regarding the Seattle burlesque incident.
subfiles.summary: R. Walton Moore replies to Neville's telegram No. 167 concerning the August 9 representation of the Emperor of Japan in Seattle. The instruction summarizes Counselor Yoshizawa's August 10 call at the Department, during which Yoshizawa emphasized that the Japanese Consul had approached the Mayor of Seattle and hoped for a local adjustment rather than a formal protest. Moore encloses a copy of Under Secretary Phillips's memorandum of conversation of August 14 with Ambassador Saito, in which the incident was further reviewed.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 827 to Edwin L. Neville Concerning the Seattle Incident

subfiles.about: A copy of Under Secretary William Phillips's memorandum of August 14 detailing his discussion with Ambassador Saito regarding the Seattle incident.
subfiles.summary: This document is a duplicate file copy of Under Secretary William Phillips's memorandum of conversation with Ambassador Hirosi Saito dated August 14, 1935. It details Saito's visit under instructions from the Foreign Office to raise the Seattle street burlesque while avoiding the word 'protest.' Phillips concurred that the Mayor of Seattle's apology should have settled the matter and referred Saito to Secretary Hull's public remarks on the Vanity Fair affair, with which Saito expressed satisfaction.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between William Phillips and Ambassador Hirosi Saito (Enclosure Copy)

subfiles.about: Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville provides a comprehensive analysis of the Japanese press and official reaction to the Vanity Fair caricature of Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.summary: Edwin L. Neville reports on the public and official reaction in Japan to the Vanity Fair cartoon, noting that the controversy was largely whipped up by the Tokyo Asahi and Osaka Asahi to capitalize on a shortage of domestic news. The Japanese government banned the August issue and ordered its confiscation, while newspaper pressure forced Foreign Minister Hirota to instruct Ambassador Saito to intervene. Neville notes that the press never described the cartoon itself, creating an exaggerated sense of insult, and misrepresented Secretary Hull's statement as an unqualified apology (ikan). He concludes that Japanese press restrictions distorted the American position, placing the United States in an unfavorable light while preventing any accurate public explanation of the satire.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1428 from Tokyo on Japanese Reception of the Vanity Fair Caricature

subfiles.about: Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville analyzes the Japanese Cabinet's August 3 statement condemning Dr. Minobe's institutional theory of the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports on the official statement issued by the Okada Cabinet on August 3, 1935, defining the constitutional position of the Emperor following attacks on Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's 'organ theory' initiated by Baron Takeo Kikuchi in the House of Peers. The despatch includes a full English translation of the Cabinet statement, which affirmed that supreme authority resides indivisibly in the Emperor in accordance with the divine command of the Sun Goddess and the Meiji Constitution. Neville analyzes this development as a major triumph for imperial fundamentalists and the military, reflecting a regressive political trend since the 1931 Manchurian incident to reinforce State Shinto and suppress academic constitutional interpretation. He adds that while the government hoped the pronouncement would appease extremists without requiring criminal prosecution of Minobe, Premier Okada defended Privy Council President Baron Ikki against similar political attacks.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1429 from Tokyo on Japanese Government Statement on the Position of the Emperor

subfiles.about: An extract from the Japan Monthly Political Report for July 1935 (Despatch No. 1422) regarding political agitation over the Minobe organ theory, accompanied by a cross-reference sheet and routing slip.
subfiles.summary: This subfile consists of a Document File Note cross-referencing Despatch No. 1422 (Japan Political Report for July 1935), a two-page excerpt from Section III on Internal Political Affairs, and a routing slip. The extract reviews political developments during July 1935 surrounding Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's theory that the Emperor is an organ of state. It describes Premier Keisuke Okada's defense of Privy Council President Baron Ikki, the resulting suspicion in military circles, War Minister General Senjuro Hayashi's ultimatum to the Cabinet, and petitions by General Kunishige Tanaka of the right-wing Meirinkai society and the Seiyukai party demanding government suppression of the theory.
subfiles.title: Despatch Extract and Document File Note: Internal Political Affairs: The Emperor

subfiles.about: Stanley K. Hornbeck thanks the editor of The Dallas Morning News for sending an editorial on the Vanity Fair controversy and clarifies the Department's official statement.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges receipt of copies of the editorial page of The Dallas Morning News containing an editorial titled 'Too Sensitive.' To clarify the facts regarding the meeting between Secretary Hull and the Japanese Ambassador on August 5, Hornbeck quotes the full press release issued by the State Department. The release states that Hull noted the publisher's denial of any intent to offend and expressed general regret whenever incidents arise that cause misunderstanding between nations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to the Editor of The Dallas Morning News
subfiles.to: The Editor, The Dallas Morning News

subfiles.about: An editorial from The Dallas Morning News criticizing the State Department for expressing regret over the Vanity Fair cartoon and urging Japan not to be overly sensitive.
subfiles.summary: The editorial discusses the Japanese protest over the Vanity Fair cartoon of Emperor Hirohito, comparing it to China's imprisonment of the editor of the New Life magazine under Japanese pressure. The editorial argues that while the U.S. government correctly explained that it exercises no control over the American press, it erred in expressing official regret, thereby creating a bad precedent. It asserts that heads of state in democratic societies are routine subjects for cartoonists and concludes that Japan must learn to accept foreign humor rather than expecting the world to bow to its sacred taboos.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Editorial: 'Too Sensitive' (The Dallas Morning News)

subfiles.about: Consul Samuel Sokobin reports on the apology published by the Tsingtao Shih Pao for reprinting news of the Seattle disrespect incident and analyzes local Japanese pressure.
subfiles.summary: Samuel Sokobin reports to Minister Johnson regarding an apology published by the leading Chinese newspaper Tsingtao Shih Pao for reprinting an account of the Seattle burlesque of the Japanese Emperor. Sokobin explains that while the Seattle stunt itself was trivial, the incident highlights the extreme lengths to which Chinese municipal authorities go to placate Japanese sensitivities and avoid military trouble. Enclosed are translations of the Tsingtao Shih Pao's apology and the original news item, which recounted the Seattle parade and the Shanghai ban on Vanity Fair. Sokobin notes that local Chinese and Japanese newspapers used the phrase bujing shijian (case of disrespect / lèse-majesté), and observes that municipal authorities had issued strict circular orders barring publication.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 319 from American Consulate at Tsingtao on Chinese Newspaper Apology

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson transmits Shanghai Despatch No. 8802 containing memoranda of conversations between Consul General Cunningham, Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki, and Shanghai police officials.
subfiles.summary: Minister Nelson T. Johnson forwards to Secretary Hull Despatch No. 8802 of August 10, 1935, from Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham in Shanghai, approving Cunningham's refusal to assist Japanese suppression of Vanity Fair. The enclosures comprise three detailed memoranda of conversations held by Cunningham. In meetings on August 7 and 8, Japanese Vice Consul Terasaki requested Cunningham to ask the Shanghai Municipal Council police to suppress and seize the August Vanity Fair; Cunningham firmly refused, citing his duty to protect American commercial interests and press freedom, while comparing Japanese reverence for the Emperor to American reverence for the national flag. In an August 9 meeting with Deputy Commissioner T. P. Givens of the Shanghai Municipal Police Special Branch, Cunningham rejected police proposals to request booksellers not to sell the magazine, reprimanding the police for attempting to act as censors of American publications.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3767 from Peiping Transmitting Shanghai Despatch on Vanity Fair

subfiles.about: Captain W. D. Puleston, Director of Naval Intelligence, provides Stanley K. Hornbeck with intelligence reports from Hawaii concerning Japanese reactions to the Vanity Fair cartoon and royal family coverage.
subfiles.summary: Captain W. D. Puleston, Director of Naval Intelligence, writes to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck quoting intelligence reports from Hawaii. He cites an article from the Japanese-English newspaper Hawaii Hochi interpreting Secretary Hull's statement as a formal apology and expressing congratulations that the Vanity Fair incident was settled. Puleston also includes a report from the Commandant of the Naval Station, Hawaii, recalling that when a reader wrote to the Honolulu Advertiser criticizing reverent coverage of the Japanese Imperial Prince's birth as un-American, local Japanese business organisations considered boycotting the newspaper.
subfiles.title: Letter from Captain W. D. Puleston (ONI) to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck on Japanese-American Sentiment

subfiles.about: Consul General Cunningham transmits a report and editorial from The China Press discussing local press subservience to Japanese influence following the Vanity Fair affair.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham transmits to Secretary Hull a copy of his Despatch No. 8833 to the Legation at Peiping analyzing Shanghai press reactions to the Vanity Fair controversy. Cunningham observes that Chinese newspapers dare not criticize Japan and English-language papers practice voluntary self-censorship due to Japan's dominant position. Enclosed is a sycophantic editorial from The China Press titled 'Big Splash,' which compares the Japanese Foreign Office to Heracles fighting the Hydra as the cartoon spread worldwide, while praising Japanese indignation, condemning Gropper's cartoons, and attacking Japanese writer Takano Murobushi for criticizing Japan's aggressive policy in China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8836 from Shanghai Transmitting Despatch No. 8833 on Local Editorial Comment

subfiles.about: An extract from Canton Despatch No. 59 (Political Report for August 1935) and accompanying Document File Note detailing Japanese efforts to ban Vanity Fair in Canton.
subfiles.summary: This subfile consists of a Document File Note cross-referencing Canton Despatch No. 59 of September 9, 1935, and an extract describing Japanese attempts to suppress the August Vanity Fair in Canton. Japanese Vice Consul Hattori asked the Commissioner of Customs to confiscate copies upon arrival, but the Commissioner refused without orders from Nanking. Hattori then warned Canton municipal and provincial authorities that Japan would react severely if the cartoon were reproduced in Kwangtung, contrasting Japan's expected response with that taken in the United States. The report notes that Japanese consular pressure across China aims to instill among the Chinese the same awe and reverence for the Emperor that exists in Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch Extract and Document File Note: Attempt to Suppress Vanity Fair in Canton

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 1501 on the outcome of the Minobe constitutional theory controversy and recommending an attached article by Hugh Byas.
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 1501 regarding the controversy over Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's institutional theory of the Emperor. The memorandum notes the Embassy's conclusion that the military won an emphatic victory in the Minobe issue, supported by widespread public backing for the fundamentalist theory of the Emperor. Turner calls attention to an insightful analysis by journalist Hugh Byas appended to the despatch and recommends it to Division officers.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1501 Regarding the Minobe Controversy
subfiles.to: Eugene H. Dooman, Maxwell M. Hamilton, Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: Despatch No. 1501 from Tokyo reporting developments in the Minobe constitutional theory controversy, including Minobe's resignation from the House of Peers and continued military pressure.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1501 from Tokyo reports further developments in the dispute over Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's theory that the Emperor is an organ of state. Despite the Cabinet's August 3 statement condemning the theory, the military continued agitating for severe action, with the War and Navy Ministers declaring at an Ex-Service Men's Association rally that the theory violated national polity. In early September, Justice Ministry authorities moved to prosecute Minobe under Article 26 of the Publication Law, dropping charges only after Minobe resigned from the House of Peers on September 17. When Minobe asserted publicly that he resigned due to peer pressure rather than changing his views, newly appointed War Minister General Kawashima demanded another Cabinet statement, which Premier Okada refused on September 19.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1501 from Tokyo: Controversy Over the Institutional Theory of the Japanese Emperor
